passage: I'm Jyoti, and I still think about that Ganesh visarjan night with Rehana. The street was packed, drums going, strangers hugging and jumping with their arms in the air. Rehana grabbed my hands and we spun, laughing till our faces hurt. It felt like everybody was one happy body. Then the mood shifted. Somebody near the back started shoving to get closer to the truck, and the shoulders around us stopped swaying and turned hard. I saw Rehana's smile go tight. We had already agreed on the lane by the pharmacy as our way out, so we slipped along the edge and stood there catching our breath. I was sad to leave, but glad we had a plan.

qa.q: Which lane had Jyoti and Rehana agreed on as their way out?
qa.a: They had agreed on the lane by the pharmacy.

qa.q: What did Jyoti feel when the crowd's mood shifted?
qa.a: Jyoti felt uneasy and tense, seeing the shoulders turn hard and Rehana's smile go tight. Jyoti was also sad to leave, so the feelings were mixed.

qa.q: What was wise about how Jyoti and Rehana handled the crowd?
qa.a: They noticed the mood change early and used the exit they had agreed on, rather than staying to see if it calmed.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt when the pushing began?
qa.a: Rehana's smile going tight suggests worry, though Rehana may also have been reluctant to end the fun, so leaving quietly respected both feelings.

grounding: A young adult reads jumping, hugging and dancing at a festival as shared joy, then notices the crowd shift and uses an exit plan.

passage: Coach's note, Saturday, district football final. From my seat by the pitch I saw the crowd behind the goal cheering hard when Chaitanya scored: jumping, arms round each other, a few people dancing on the steps. That was ordinary joy. Chaitanya, still in the stands after being subbed, was clapping and hugging a teammate. Later, when we equalised late, the noise changed. People started pushing along the rail. Chaitanya glanced at the staircase, tapped the teammate's arm and the two of them moved to the side exit. I didn't tell them to. I'm Pradeep, the coach, and next week I'll go over exit points with the whole squad, so leaving early is normal.

qa.q: Where did Chaitanya go when the noise changed?
qa.a: Chaitanya and a teammate moved to the side exit.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya likely feeling when glancing at the staircase?
qa.a: Chaitanya was probably uneasy about the pushing along the rail, and chose safety over staying for the celebration. A different reading is that Chaitanya just wanted to beat the rush, since the note cannot say.

qa.q: What could Pradeep do so players know how to handle a crowd?
qa.a: Go over exit points with the whole squad and make it normal to leave early when the mood shifts.

qa.q: How might the teammate have felt about leaving?
qa.a: The teammate may have wanted to stay for the celebration, but followed after Chaitanya's tap, which suggests trust.

grounding: A coach sees crowd joy at a match turn into unsafe pushing and a player moves to an exit.

subtype: Ducking and defensive reflex in danger [Regulating]
passage: Note from Mr. Mridul, campus safety volunteer. On Friday evening I was at the crossing outside the gate when two motorbike riders began shouting at each other over a near-miss. A crowd gathered. Sumit, a first-year student who had stopped to wait for the light, dropped low, covered the back of the head with one arm and stepped back behind a parked auto. I saw the crouch as a quick protective move, not fear alone. When one rider grabbed the other's collar, Sumit walked off and phoned the guard post. Afterwards I told Sumit that leaving early was the sensible choice, and I asked whether a short safety session for first-years would help. Sumit said it would.

qa.a: Mridul saw it at the crossing outside the gate.

qa.a: Sumit moved away early and phoned the guard post, rather than trying to intervene or prove anything.

qa.a: The crowd could have made the argument worse or kept it going, which is why getting help and leaving is safer than joining in.

subtype: Ducking and defensive reflex in danger [Regulating]
passage: Diary, 11 pm. Joseph writing. Outside the tea stall today Reena and I saw two guys arguing over a parked scooter. It got loud fast. One of them kept shouting, "Say it again!" and the other stepped right up to his face. My body did something before my brain did: my shoulders dropped, my hands came up near my head and I took a step back. Reena tugged my sleeve and said, "Let's go." We crossed to the other side, and Reena texted the shop owner that there was a fight starting. I felt shaky after, and a bit silly, but I'm glad we didn't stay. Walking away wasn't losing.

qa.a: The shop owner probably saw it as a helpful warning so they could keep customers safe or call for help.

grounding: A young adult ducks and steps away when a fight risk appears, and leaving early and getting help protects better than bravado.

When Neel's phone buzzed, Hrithik glanced at it, then away, and gave a smile that stopped before his eyes. Maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing to do with Neel. I couldn't tell. Afterwards I texted him, "Want to grab tea, just us? No pressure." He said yes, and I said I'd listen and that I'd help find someone to talk to if he wanted. I'm Tejas, and I don't want to guess for him.

qa.a: Tejas seems concerned but careful, unsure whether it was tiredness or something about Neel, so Tejas offers tea and listening rather than guessing for Hrithik.

subtype: Covering the mouth and cultural norms [Mismatch]
passage: Diary, Sunday night. Two things today. At my cousin's wedding in Pune I covered my mouth when I laughed, like I always do, and Alka teased me about it: "Bhupen, you giggle like a schoolgirl." I felt my ears warm. In my family it's manners, we all do it, my mother especially. But Alka said her friends from Kerala laugh with their whole faces and nobody hides anything. Later at dinner an older guest yawned and put his hand over his mouth, exactly the same move, and I realised it's just politeness there. I asked Alka if she thought it looked shy. She said, "Only a bit. It's kind of cute." I think I'll keep doing it. 🙂

qa.a: The wedding was in Pune.

qa.a: Ask a friend how it comes across, and keep the habit if it feels natural, since its meaning depends on the setting.

qa.q: How does Alka see the mouth covering?
qa.a: Alka finds it a bit shy but cute, and knows friends from Kerala who laugh with their whole faces, so norms differ.

grounding: A young adult covers the mouth when laughing or yawning, meaning manners in one setting and shyness in another.

passage: I'm Ankita, and looking back, my first year of college was the year I stopped apologising for how I move. I've always rocked a little when I concentrate and flapped my hands when a new idea excites me. At school I was told it was rude, that I looked like I wasn't paying attention. So I sat on my hands. My grades slipped, because I was concentrating on hiding. Then Jyoti, my lab partner, saw me rocking during a tough problem and simply said, "That looks like it helps." I nearly cried. I told her yes, it does, it's how I think. Now I move in class, quietly, and I listen better than I ever did.

qa.q: What did Ankita do at school because she was told it was rude?
qa.a: Ankita sat on her hands.

qa.q: What did Ankita feel when Jyoti said 'That looks like it helps'?
qa.a: Ankita felt relieved and understood, enough to nearly cry, since her movement was finally seen as useful rather than rude. It may also have felt like an unexpected kindness after years of hiding.

qa.q: What might a teacher do differently when a student rocks or flaps in class?
qa.a: Ask what helps the student focus instead of assuming inattention, and allow quiet movement.

qa.q: How did Jyoti see Ankita's rocking?
qa.a: Jyoti saw it as something that helped Ankita concentrate on a tough problem, and said so plainly without judging it.

grounding: A young adult uses rocking and hand flapping as regulation to focus, and others should not read it as rudeness.

passage:
Manoj sat on the balcony of the Andheri flat with his laptop, frowning at a bug that wouldn't go away. Siddharth came out with two mugs of tea and put one beside him. Manoj rubbed his eyes.

"Long day?" Siddharth asked. Manoj nodded.

"Can I?" Siddharth held his hand near Manoj's hair, not touching. "Only if you want it."

"Yes, please."

He ran his fingers lightly through Manoj's hair a few times. Manoj's shoulders dropped and he leaned in a little, eyes closing. After a minute Manoj said, "That's enough, thanks," and Siddharth stopped at once, squeezed his shoulder, and picked up the tea.

qa.a: Siddharth asked first, kept the hand still until Manoj said yes, and stopped at once when Manoj said enough.

qa.q: What could Siddharth have done if Manoj had stiffened or said no?
qa.a: Siddharth could have pulled back, put the hand down and checked in gently about what Manoj needed instead.

"Can I sit here?" Maria asked, dropping her bag on the sofa.
"Of course," said Simran. "Bad exam?"
"Awful. I froze on the last question." Maria's voice wobbled. "Is it okay if I put my head on your shoulder for a bit?"
"Sure. Come here."
Simran stroked Maria's hair a few times, slowly. Then Maria's shoulders tensed.
"Too much?" Simran asked, pulling her hand back at once.
"A little. Just sit with me instead."
"Okay. I'm right here."
They watched the rain run down the window for a while. Maria breathed out. "Thanks for checking. Sometimes I want closeness, sometimes I don't."
"I'll always ask," said Simran.

Wednesday. In the corridor Hemant grabbed Raghav's arm again. Raghav raised his palm and said firmly, "No. Don't touch me." Hemant kept his hand there for a second. Raghav pulled his arm free with a light push and stepped away, heart racing, and walked into the staff room.

passage: Jaya, come and sit. I want to tell you something from when I was twenty. There was a boy in my hostel, Deepak, who liked to put his arm around every girl's shoulder. I told him once, politely, "Please don't." He just grinned. So the next time I put my hand up flat, stepped back and said, "I said no." My knees were shaking, but my voice wasn't. He went red and let go. I still went to the warden that evening and told her, because one no isn't always enough. I'm Uma, and I've learned that you never owe anyone your comfort. Step away, say it clearly, and tell someone you trust.

qa.q: What did Uma do with her hand when she said no the second time?
qa.a: Uma put her hand up flat and stepped back.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she said 'I said no'?
qa.a: Uma was frightened, as her shaking knees show, but she was also determined and kept her voice steady. Deepak's going red shows he understood the boundary.

qa.q: What could a young person do if someone ignores a clear no?
qa.a: Step away, say it again clearly, and tell a trusted person such as a warden, teacher or counsellor.

qa.a: Jaya may feel reassured that saying no is allowed, or nervous about speaking up, so hearing that Uma's knees shook too may help.

passage: Rosa stepped up to the ticket window in Rotterdam and heard Tariq breathing behind her. She glanced back. The woman behind Tariq raised her eyebrows and moved back to leave more gap. Rosa hadn't meant to seem cold, she just liked space. Tariq noticed the shuffle and felt a flash of hurt, then remembered the guidebook line about personal space. He took a small step back, smiled and said, "Sorry, I'm still learning." Rosa laughed and said, "No problem. It's just different."
